items.title: Joe Watkins Interview, 1969-03-24
items.q: But it was him, Lee Armstrong, Funk Johnson, and you had Manuel Moneta.

ctx.x: Okay, well we're interviewing Joe Watkins this March 24th, 1969. Just going from what you're about to say, Joe, about when you started music.

When I started, I started in 1920s. Well that was quite a few years after George Lewis and Paul Barbrain. Well I always did love drums because I was born in the third ward and that was, a section for jazz probably because Lee Armstrong was from that ward. He was born and raised around there. And I don't know about Joe Oliver because I always heard that Joe was not exactly from the Orlins. But it was him, Lee Armstrong, Funk Johnson, and you had Manuel Moneta. And, uh, was this other fella's name, uh, was a good…
What sort of date was this? Huh? What date was this about?

items.title: Joe Watkins Interview, 1961-01-20
items.q: And them days, Bunk Johnson was playing there.

ctx.x: And them days, Bunk Johnson was playing there. That was on Saturday nights. Every Saturday night they had a dance sometime, they'd have them on Sunday nights. Remember who was with Bunk in that family? No, because I was too small. See, I was too small at that time to remember who was playing with them.
But just the sixth grade was...

items.title: Joe Watkins Interview, 1960-03-16
items.q: and Bunk was playing, used to play that too, I'm more than sure

ctx.x: But that place you said, what street was it on, between St. Louis and Quarantine?

Right on the corner, at Liberty and Quarantine. Liberty, oh. Yeah, right on the corner, second catacomb from St. Louis Street Cemetery, yeah. Well I had the opportunity to get in to Lula White's place, and Emma Johnson and Willa Piazza, I used to deliver drinks to those different places, and naturally it was good money in them days, the salary wasn't much but the tips were so great, you know. Well I did fairly good, and I left from there, and right after they closed the district down in 1916 I think it was. And…
